newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus PM stands down as crisis deepens.
newsitem.headline: Belarus PM stands down as crisis deepens.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, locked in a fierce battle for power with parliament, said on Monday he had accepted the resignation of his prime minister, Mikhail Chigir.

Lukashenko, accused by critics of trying to set up a dictatorship in the former Soviet republic, told state television the current deputy prime minister responsible for economic and finance issues, Sergei Ling, would replace Chigir.
The 42-year-old president, who hopes to boost his powers in a referendum that ends on Sunday, said his labour minister Alexander Sosnov had also resigned from the government.
Earlier Chigir met parliamentary leaders who quoted him as saying he would resign unless Lukashenko cancelled his referendum.
Lukashenko made clear in his television interview that he had no plans to do this.
"I am saying for the last time -- it is time to understand the train has already left. It will not be stopped, the referendum will happen," he said.
Chigir, who had remained loyal to Lukashenko during months of escalating tension, stepped down as members of parliament began impeachment moves against the president.
The parliament is due to meet again on Tuesday and has invited the president to attend the session.

Chigir is a well-respected figure in the republic of 10 million people. Lukashenko appointed him prime minister after winning a landslide election in July 1994 with promises to wipe out corruption and rebuild ties with neighbouring Russia.
His departure could deal a big blow to Lukashenko's campaign to tighten his grip on rival institutions, including parliament and the constitutional court, political analysts said.
On Monday Lukashenko was in characteristically defiant mood, telling his opponents they should be ready to flee Belarus if he wins the referendum, which would extend his term by more than two years.
"Whoever doesn't want this will have to find another motherland...I am not trying to scare anyone but that's how it will be," he told a rally in the southern city of Gomel.
About 200 anti-Lukashenko demonstrators kept up a vigil outside parliament late on Monday, cheering speeches which were relayed by loudspeaker to Independence Square.
Lukashenko's top aide, Vladimir Zametalin, told Reuters the president could stop parliament impeaching him even if the constitutional court approved such a decision.
"The president of the republic will use the maximum possibilities available to him to get out of the situation without conflict," Zametalin said in a telephone interview.
Asked if this could include dissolving parliament and the constitutional court, he said: "It's entirely possible. The president has many options."

If the constitutional court approved the deputies' impeachment moves, 132 members of parliament would have to vote in favour of the decision. Only 108 deputies, including some who back Lukashenko, attended Monday's session.

In Paris, members of the North Atlantic Assembly, which groups parliamentarians from 40 European and North American countries including the 16 NATO states, voiced strong support for the Belarus parliament against Lukashenko.
Assembly president Karsten Voigt of Germany told a news conference that Lukashenko's behaviour was "illegal, non-democratic and sometimes even crazy".
